rows.reply:
Two sentences tie for longest, both at twelve words: "Behind her, Tomas lit a cigarette and thought she was being ridiculous" and "She could still see the color of his coat at the rail." So I'll take them both, briefly.

The Tomas sentence could lose about two words — "and thought she was ridiculous" instead of "and thought she was being ridiculous." But "being ridiculous" and "ridiculous" aren't the same judgement. "Being ridiculous" says she's doing something, making a performance of it, which she could stop; "ridiculous" says she is that way. The first is the more dismissive of the two, and it's the one you have. The other thing that sentence does is hang his dismissal off the same breath as the cigarette — one easy motion, lighting up and writing her off. If you split it into two sentences you'd get sharpness but lose that offhandedness. So: shorter is available, at a cost I'd think hard about.

The last sentence could go to nine — "She could still see his coat at the rail" — but "the color of" is doing work three sentences earlier. The water is pewter, grey, no colour to speak of, and what she can still pick out is that his coat has colour, without you saying which. That's a real thing happening in the passage and the cut would take it out. "Still" is also holding the minute she asked for.

So my honest answer is: a word or two, not more, and each cut buys speed with something specific. The passage is already running short — six, eight, six words — and those two twelve-word sentences are where it breathes out. Cutting them tighter might flatten the difference rather than tighten the whole.

Worth weighing before you cut, though: this sentence's length is what makes "Then it slowed to a whisper on the slate. Then it stopped. Silence." land as a contraction. Tighten it much and the three short sentences have less to contract from. A light trim keeps that shape; a hard one flattens it.

rows.ask: Tighten the first sentence for me.
rows.reply:
The slack I can see is mostly in three places. "long" is doing work that "All through the ... afternoon" already does, so it is the easiest word to lose. "worked its way" is a slower verb than the sentence strictly needs, and gives you two prepositional runs, along and down, before the sentence lands. And "the cracked pane of the kitchen window" is a three-step chain that could be compressed to two if you let the kitchen modify the pane directly.

Worth weighing against that: the length of this sentence is what makes the three that follow feel like a drop. If it tightens too far, "Then it slowed to a whisper on the slate. Then it stopped. Silence." loses the long thing it is shortening against. Cutting "long" alone keeps the shape and removes the redundancy.

This is Line work, on the sentence as it now stands: "Then it slowed to a whisper on the slate."

Two places it could give. Dropping the verb phrase — "Then a whisper on the slate" — removes three words and makes the sentence a bare image, which puts it closer in texture to "Silence" at the end; the cost is that "slowed" is the only word carrying the movement from the long first sentence into the stop. Dropping the location instead — "Then it slowed to a whisper" — also removes three words, but slate is the one new surface after gutters and pane, and losing it means the rain has nowhere left to be heard.

Worth saying too that at nine words it is already the shortest of the three full sentences, and the paragraph's descent depends on it being longer than "Then it stopped" and shorter than the first. rows.ask: Tighten the second sentence for me.
rows.reply:
As it stands the sentence is already lean — nine words, and most of them are carrying something. The two places where words could come out are "to a whisper" and "on the slate". Dropping the second gives you "Then it slowed to a whisper," which keeps the sound and the slowing but loses the slate, and with it the third surface after the gutters and the pane; the rain stops moving up onto the roof. Dropping the first and folding the sound into the verb gives you "Then it whispered on the slate," six words, which keeps the roof and the hush but loses the sense of it easing off, which is what makes the next sentence's "Then it stopped" feel earned.

Either way I'd keep "Then", since it's what makes the second and third sentences fall together.

rows.reply:
You're at the level of how the sentences move, so that's where I'll answer.

The longest sentence is the first, at twenty-two words, and what it does is largely a function of that length. "All through the long afternoon" declares a long span, and the sentence then takes its time crossing one — the rain travels along the gutters and then down the pane, two movements chained by "and," so the reading of it lasts. Everything after it shortens: eight words, then three, then one. The first sentence is the height the rest falls from.

The modifiers — "long," "cracked," "kitchen" — are specifying detail rather than structural; losing them would take three words off and the diminishing would survive intact, though "cracked" is the only image of damage in the passage and the window would become plainer. rows.ask: Tighten the first sentence for me.

claims.text: "Mara watched the ferry pull away" is six words
claims.detail: said 6, "Mara watched the ferry pull away" has 6

rows.reply:
This is at the level of the sentence. "Mara watched the ferry pull away" is six words with nothing idle in it. The only removable piece is "pull": "Mara watched the ferry leave" saves one word but loses the drag of a boat working against water, which is the only physical motion in the line. A bigger cut would be "The ferry pulled away" — three words gone, but it takes Mara out of the subject position, and the rest of the paragraph is held in her watching, so the opening would no longer be hers.

My honest reading is that there is little slack here to take. If the sentence feels heavy to you, it may not be length but position — it does the work of establishing her, the ferry and the watching all at once, and a sentence can feel slow doing three jobs even when it is short.

rows.ask: How much shorter could the longest sentence get without losing what it does?
rows.reply:
This is the sentence level — how the sentences move.

Checking it word by word, two sentences tie at twelve words: "Behind her, Tomas lit a cigarette and thought she was being ridiculous" and "She could still see the color of his coat at the rail." Neither is longer than the other by count, though the Tomas sentence runs longer on the page.

What each length is doing is different. In the Tomas sentence, the "and" hinges an outward act onto an inward judgement, and that hinge is the only place the narration steps out of Mara's head. Shortening it means either dropping the cigarette or dropping the thought; the first costs you the gesture that makes him physically present behind her, the second costs you the only other consciousness in the paragraph. So the twelve words are carrying two jobs, and there isn't much slack between them.
